scenes.narration: Python has a special method named init, with two underscores on each side. It runs automatically, the moment an object is created. Inside it, you store data on the object with self dot name equals name. The words after self are the arguments you pass when you build the object. Think of a form every new student fills in at the door. Nobody enters the class without name and marks. The values stored on the object are called attributes.

scenes.narration: [HL 1] The Student blueprint. [HL 2] The special method init. Self first, then the values we want. [HL 3] Store the name on this object. [HL 4] Store the marks on this object. [HL 6] Build a student with a name and marks. Python calls init for us, and passes the arguments after self. [HL 7] A second student. [HL 8] Asha ninety one. [HL 9] Ravi seventy eight. [HL 10] We can change an attribute later. [HL 11] Asha is now ninety five, and Ravi is still seventy eight.

code.source:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        self.name = name
        self.marks = marks

a = Student("Asha", 91)
b = Student("Ravi", 78)
print(a.name, a.marks)
print(b.name, b.marks)
a.marks = 95
print(a.marks, b.marks)

scenes.onScreen: The names a and b tied to two Student objects, each holding its own name and marks

scenes.narration: Here is the picture. The name a is tied to one student object. Inside it live two attributes, name and marks. The name b is tied to another student, with its own attributes. Same blueprint, different data. Init filled both objects in, at the moment they were born.

scenes.onScreen: rectangle.py: init with a default value, and a method that uses the attributes
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A Rectangle class. [HL 2] Init takes a width, and a height that defaults to one. [HL 3] Store the width. [HL 4] Store the height. [HL 6] A method named area. [HL 7] It multiplies the two attributes of this object, and returns the answer. [HL 9] Four by three. [HL 10] Five, with the default height of one. [HL 11] Twelve. [HL 12] Five. [HL 13] And the default height is one.

code.source:
class Rectangle:
    def __init__(self, width, height=1):
        self.width = width
        self.height = height

    def area(self):
        return self.width * self.height

r1 = Rectangle(4, 3)
r2 = Rectangle(5)
print(r1.area())
print(r2.area())
print(r2.height)

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: forgot self. on the attribute
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We wrote name equals name, without self dot. That creates a plain local variable, which vanishes when init ends. The object has no name at all. So s dot name raises an attribute error, Student object has no attribute name. Always write self dot, to store data on the object.

shorts.title: self dot name
shorts.hook: "Inside init, write self dot name equals name."
shorts.script: Inside init, write self dot name equals name. That stores the value on the object, as an attribute. Without the self dot, the value is only a local variable, and it vanishes. Self dot is what makes data stick to the object. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Self dot makes data stick.

shorts.title: Passing arguments
shorts.hook: "When you write Student with Asha and ninety one in brackets, Python builds the object and calls init."
shorts.script: When you write Student with Asha and ninety one in brackets, Python builds the object and calls init. The two values go into init after self. Each object you build gets its own name and marks, stored in its own attributes. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Arguments go to init.

shorts.title: The missing self
shorts.script: A silent beginner bug. In init you write name equals name, with no self dot. No error yet. Later you print s dot name, and Python says, attribute error, Student object has no attribute name. The value was never stored on the object. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Always write self dot.
